details.readme:
![claude-bughunter banner](assets/banner-v2.svg) # claude-bughunter > A self-contained Claude skill bundle for bug hunting and external red-team work · **83 skills** · 15 slash commands · **681 disclosed-report patterns** (433 now individually cited & auditable) across 24 core vulnerability classes · enterprise identity + infrastructure attack matrices · engagement-folder scaffolding · Burp MCP integration · battle-tested across authorized red-team and bug-hunting engagements, plus public training platforms (DVWA, OWASP Juice Shop, Hacker101, testphp.vulnweb.com). Built by **[Sachin Sharma](https://www.linkedin.com/in/sachinsharma8080/)** — Bug Hunting & GenAI Security Research.

SPONSORED BY
    

--- ## What is this? `claude-bughunter` is a drop-in skill bundle for the [Claude Code skills system](https://docs.claude.com/en/docs/claude-code/skills). Install once and Claude Code stops being a chatbot and starts behaving like a senior bug-hunting researcher or red-team operator: it knows the techniques, the chain templates, the VRT mappings, the platform CVE chains, and the hygiene — and it stays in scope. Four layers stack: - **Think** — `bb-methodology` + `redteam-mindset`: the 5-phase non-linear workflow, critical-thinking framework, and red-team operator discipline. - **Hunt webapps** — 58 `hunt-*` skills curated from 681 disclosed HackerOne reports: per-class detection patterns, payloads, bypass tables, and chain templates. - **Hit the perimeter** — enterprise platform chains (M365/Entra, Okta, vCenter, SSL-VPN appliances, SharePoint, cloud IAM): current 2024–2026 CVE chains + post-credential escalation. - **Ship it** — `triage-validation` + reporting + `evidence-hygiene`: the 7-Question Gate, VRT-aware severity, OOS rebuttals, PII redaction, and red-team deliverables. All triggered automatically by topic — describe what you're testing in plain English and the relevant skill loads. No invocation by name. --- ## Quickstart **Option A — install as a Claude Code plugin (recommended).** From inside Claude Code: ```text /plugin marketplace add elementalsouls/Claude-BugHunter /plugin install claude-bughunter@elementalsouls ``` All 83 skills + 15 commands load namespaced under `claude-bughunter:` and update when you bump the plugin version — no files copied into `~/.claude/`. **A HackerOne account is optional.** The install asks for a HackerOne API username and token. They only let the HackerOne MCP read your private programs and your own reports; leave both blank if you don't need that. Every skill, command and the MCP's public tools (duplicate search, program scope) work without them. **Option B — copy install (no plugin system / pin to a clone):** ```bash git clone https://github.com/elementalsouls/Claude-BugHunter.git cd Claude-BugHunter ``` ```bash # macOS / Linux bash scripts/install.sh # Windows (PowerShell) pwsh ./scripts/install.ps1 ``` Both copy the skills + commands into `~/.claude/` (macOS/Linux) or `%USERPROFILE%\.claude\` (Windows) and wire the `hunt` engagement scaffolder. **What each install path gives you:** | Path | 83 skills + 15 slash commands | `cbh` CLI | `hunt` scaffolder | |---|---|---|---| | **A — plugin** | ✅ namespaced under `claude-bughunter:` | ➕ separate `pipx install` | ❌ clone-only | | **B — copy install** | ✅ copied into `~/.claude/` | ✅ from the clone | ✅ from the clone | The plugin is the fastest path to the skills + slash commands. The terminal-native `cbh` runner installs standalone — `pipx install git+https://github.com/elementalsouls/Claude-BugHunter` — so plugin users can add it without a full clone (see [`cbh` CLI](docs/cbh-cli.md)). The `hunt` engagement scaffolder ships with the clone (Option B). That's it. Open Claude Code and describe what you're testing in plain English — the right skill loads automatically, no invocation by name: ```text > Testing acme.com — an in-scope HackerOne target. Run recon and rank the surface. ⟳ loading skills: web2-recon, offensive-osint, bb-methodology … → subdomain enum (subfinder + crt.sh) … 47 hosts → live hosts (httpx) … 12 · tech fingerprint … 6 distinct stacks → ranked surface: api.acme.com (GraphQL, introspection ON) ← start here auth.acme.com (OAuth, SSO) ← hunt-oauth Next: want me to probe the GraphQL introspection + OAuth redirect_uri? ``` → Full [Installation guide](INSTALL.md) · [Usage guide](USAGE.md) · [searchable skill catalog](docs/skills.md). > The block above is an illustrative transcript. To record a real demo of your own session: `asciinema rec demo.cast` → upload to [asciinema.org](https://asciinema.org) and drop the badge here. --- ## Runs on multiple agent harnesses ![One install, agent harnesses — Claude Code, OpenCode, Codex CLI, Hermes Agent, Google AntiGravity](assets/harness-routing.svg) The skills are plain [Agent Skills](https://docs.claude.com/en/docs/claude-code/skills) — the same `SKILL.md` format that **Claude Code · OpenCode · OpenAI Codex CLI · Hermes Agent · Google AntiGravity** all load. One command installs them everywhere: ```bash # macOS / Linux bash scripts/install.sh --all --burp-mcp # Windows (PowerShell) pwsh ./scripts/install.ps1 -All -BurpMcp ``` | Harness | Target Skill Directory | Flag | |---|---|---| | **Claude Code** (baseline) | `~/.claude/skills/` | *(default)* | | **OpenCode** | reads `~/.claude/skills/` & `~/.agents/skills/` | *(default)* / `--agents` | | **OpenAI Codex CLI** | `~/.agents/skills/` | `--agents` | | **Hermes Agent** | `~/.hermes/skills/` | `--hermes` | | **Google AntiGravity** | `~/.gemini/config/skills/` | `--antigravity` | `--all` (`-All`) detects installed harnesses and copies skills to each harness's path (`~/.claude/skills`, `~/.agents/skills`, `~/.hermes/skills`, `~/.gemini/config/skills`); `--burp-mcp` (`-BurpMcp`) wires the Burp MCP server into each. The full *knowledge* layer ports to all five — the slash commands and `/hunt` engine stay Claude-Code-only by design. → [Multi-harness guide](docs/multi-harness.md) --- ## Star History Chart is self-hosted — regenerate with `python3 scripts/gen_star_history.py` (needs `gh auth login`). Refreshes automatically each day via `.github/workflows/star-history.yml`. --- ## Scope — what this bundle is for, and what it isn't This bundle covers the **external attack surface** — anything reachable from the internet without first compromising an internal endpoint. ### In scope - **Bug bounty hunting** — web apps, APIs, SaaS, GraphQL, OAuth, JWT, file upload, IDOR, SSRF, RCE chains - **Web application pentesting** — full hunt-* coverage of OWASP-mapped bug classes + discipline rules - **External red-team engagements** — initial-access against internet-facing enterprise estate: M365 / Entra ID, Okta-as-IdP, SharePoint on-prem (ToolShell + legacy SOAP), VMware vCenter / Workspace ONE, SSL VPN appliances (Cisco / Fortinet / Citrix / Palo Alto / Pulse / SonicWall / F5), Android APK red-team, supply-chain recon - **Cloud misconfig + post-credential escalation** — public S3, IMDS chains, STS AssumeRole, cross-account confused-deputy - **Recon + OSINT** — subdomain enum, identity-fabric mapping, certificate transparency, JS analysis, secret scanning - **Reporting** — H1, Bugcrowd (VRT-aware), Intigriti, Immunefi, plus client-facing red-team deliverable format ### Out of scope (deliberate — not gaps, design decisions) - **Internal Active Directory attacks** — BloodHound, Kerberoasting, ASREProast, DCSync, Pass-the-Hash, AD CS abuse, ntlmrelayx, Responder, PetitPotam, etc. Different operational risk profile; needs different tooling and judgment. **Future bundle, not this one.** - **C2 frameworks** — Cobalt Strike, Sliver, Mythic, Havoc, BRC4 tradecraft. Out of scope for external-only engagement model. - **Post-exploit / persistence / lateral** — Mimikatz/comsvcs LSASS dumping, golden/silver tickets, named-pipe impersonation, persistence (registry, scheduled tasks, WMI events, COM hijacking), token theft. These start after the perimeter has already broken — different bundle territory. - **Evasion** — AMSI bypass, ETW patching, AV/EDR bypass. Tied to C2 tradecraft above. - **iOS pentesting / hardware / RF / ICS** — out of scope by design. - **Binary exploitation / kernel pwn / browser internals** — different skill universe. If you're running an internal red team that includes domain-takeover chains via Kerberos or lateral movement, **this bundle won't help you in those phases** — and we'd rather say that up front than have you find out mid-engagement. The external surface handoff to internal-RT tooling (Impacket, NetExec, CrackMapExec, Rubeus, Certify, BloodHound) is intentionally outside our scope. **Coverage for internal AD and post-exploit may come in a future update.** --- ## What's inside **83 skills**, auto-loaded by topic — no invocation by name. Coverage across the external attack surface: | Category | # | Examples | |---|---|---| | Hunt — web app vuln classes | 58 | XSS, SQLi, SSRF, IDOR, LFI, SSTI, XXE, CSRF, CORS, open-redirect, SharePoint, ASP.NET/NTLM | | Enterprise platform attack ★ | 10 | M365/Entra, Okta, cloud-IAM-deep, vCenter, enterprise VPN, APK/iOS red-team pipelines, supply-chain recon | | Reporting & validation | 6 | triage-validation, evidence-hygiene, report-writing, bugcrowd-reporting | | Recon & OSINT | 5 | web2-recon, offensive-osint, osint-methodology, recon-scope-triage | | Methodology & mindset | 4 | bb-methodology, bug-bounty, redteam-mindset, bb-local-toolkit | Full searchable catalog → **[docs/skills.md](docs/skills.md)**. Also ships **15 slash commands** (`/hunt`, `/recon`, `/report`, …) and a deterministic **engagement engine** (`engine/`) that maps a target's attack surface and routes each finding to the skill that handles it. --- ## How it works A 6-phase, non-linear workflow — **recon → map & rank → hunt → validate → report** — with scope enforced in code and a **7-Question Gate** before anything is submitted. Two ways to drive it: - **Plain English** — describe what you're testing and the relevant skill loads automatically. - **`/hunt` scaffold + `cbh` CLI** — engagement-folder structure, state, and orchestration. → [Usage guide & worked example](USAGE.md) · [6-phase architecture & skill-to-phase map](docs/architecture.md) · [`cbh` CLI](docs/cbh-cli.md) --- ## Authorization These skills are intended for assets you **own** or have **written authorization to assess** (bug-bounty in-scope assets, pentest engagement letters, CTF challenges, your own infrastructure). The skills include validation gates that auto-trigger when you point Claude at unverified third-party targets — `triage-validation`'s 7-Question Gate explicitly asks whether the asset is in scope (Q3) and on the program's accepted-impact list (Q2). details.readme:
# App Store Compliance Playbook Catch App Store and Google Play rejection causes before the reviewer does. A reference and a pre-submission guard for iOS and Android apps that is plain about what a scan can prove and what still needs a person. It does not guarantee approval. Read it as a website at [mjmirza.github.io/app-store-compliance](https://mjmirza.github.io/app-store-compliance/). [![Apple App Store](https://img.shields.io/badge/Apple_App_Store-000000?logo=apple&logoColor=white)](https://developer.apple.com/app-store/review/guidelines/) [![Google Play](https://img.shields.io/badge/Google_Play-414141?logo=googleplay&logoColor=white)](https://play.google/developer-content-policy/) [![Claude Code](https://img.shields.io/badge/Claude_Code-ready-000000?logo=anthropic&logoColor=white)](#how-you-actually-use-this) [![OpenRoots ORA 2.3](https://openroots.org/badge/ora.svg)](https://openroots.org/licenses/ora/2.3) [![CI](https://img.shields.io/github/actions/workflow/status/mjmirza/app-store-compliance/ci.yml?branch=main&label=CI)](https://github.com/mjmirza/app-store-compliance/actions) [![PRs welcome](https://img.shields.io/badge/PRs-welcome-2ea44f)](.github/CONTRIBUTING.md) [![Stars](https://img.shields.io/github/stars/mjmirza/app-store-compliance?style=social)](https://github.com/mjmirza/app-store-compliance/stargazers) [![Forks](https://img.shields.io/github/forks/mjmirza/app-store-compliance?style=social)](https://github.com/mjmirza/app-store-compliance/fork) [![Follow mjmirza](https://img.shields.io/github/followers/mjmirza?label=Follow&style=social)](https://github.com/mjmirza) **If this saves you even one rejection, leave a star, fork it, and follow along. That is the whole ask.** [Star this repo](https://github.com/mjmirza/app-store-compliance)  |  [Fork it](https://github.com/mjmirza/app-store-compliance/fork)  |  [Follow on GitHub](https://github.com/mjmirza)  |  [Follow on X](https://twitter.com/MirzaJhanzaib)  |  [next8n.com](https://next8n.com)
## Start here Pick one row. The time shown is for that first step. | You are | Do this first | Time | |---|---|---| | About to submit, and you can open a terminal | Run the two commands below | 2 minutes | | Already rejected | Open [the appeal playbook](docs/MISTAKE-PATTERNS.md#the-appeal-playbook) | 10 minutes | | Not a developer | Open [the checklist](docs/PRE-SUBMISSION-CHECKLIST.md) and do its first two checks | 5 minutes | | Using an AI coding tool (Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, GitHub Copilot, Cursor, Grok, Qwen, Kimi and more), and want this on every submit | Go to [the install](#install-it-into-your-ai-coding-tool) | 1 minute | The two commands. Needs git and bash. The first downloads this playbook. The second scans your app. Nothing is installed and nothing in your app is changed. ``` git clone https://github.com/mjmirza/app-store-compliance ~/repositories/app-store-compliance bash ~/repositories/app-store-compliance/agent-os/hooks/app-store-compliance-guard.sh "/path/to/your/app" ``` Replace only `/path/to/your/app`, with the folder that holds your Xcode project or your Android app. Keep the quotes, they keep a folder name with a space in it whole. To get the path without typing it, drag the folder from Finder or your file manager into the terminal window. A small project scans in about a second, a large one can take up to a minute, and the guard prints the time it took. Findings print first, critical ones on top, each with the file and line that triggered it when there is one. The last lines tell you where you stand. | Verdict line starts with | It means | Do next | |---|---|---| | `BLOCKED.` | A critical rejection risk was found | Fix each `[CRITICAL]` line using the `fix.` line under it, then run the same command again | | `CLEAR.` | No critical risk in your code. Not an approval, the reviewer still checks what a scan cannot see | Do the account and listing checks in [the checklist](docs/PRE-SUBMISSION-CHECKLIST.md), then record them in `.app-review-readiness.json` ([why](docs/WHAT-THE-SCAN-PROVES.md)) | | `Rule pack STALE.` (near the top) | The rules this scan used are more than 60 days old | Update the playbook with `git pull`, then run the scan again | | `NOT CHECKED.` | No iOS or Android project was found in that folder, or the guard could not write its scan files. Run by hand this exits 1. As a hook it lets the command through | Point it at the right folder, and check the temp folder is writable. A managed Expo app with no native folders still gets its `app.json` or `app.config` read for purpose strings, the privacy manifest and Android permissions. Run `npx expo prebuild` to cover the native code too | ## What you get A rejection costs a week. You submit, you wait days in review, you get a one line rejection, you guess at the fix, you resubmit, you wait again. This playbook turns that loop into a check you run before you ever submit. - **You catch the rejection before Apple or Google does.** The guard runs against your project and names the risk while you can still fix it cheaply, not after a reviewer has already said no. - **You stop guessing at the cause.** Every rejection pattern maps to the exact guideline and the exact fix, so a one line rejection email becomes a known problem with a known answer. - **The two checks that cause most rejections are covered first.** A working demo account with a live backend, and a privacy declaration that matches what your app actually does at runtime, including every SDK. These are the top modern rejection causes and the playbook holds them above everything else. - **It works whether or not you write code.** A developer wires the guard into the build. A non developer reads the plain English checklist and walks the submission safely. - **Every claim is real.** Guideline numbers and statistics trace to a live Apple or Google source, never invented, so you are acting on the actual rules, not a guess. If it saves you one rejection, it has paid for the ten minutes it takes to read. ## Install it into your AI coding tool This puts the check in front of every submit. Your agent runs the guard before any submit command, such as an upload to App Store Connect or Google Play, and stops the command when a critical rejection risk stands. For a one-time scan, skip this section and use Start here. One command per tool, about a minute. Needs git and bash. Every tool other than Claude Code also needs python3. ``` git clone https://github.com/mjmirza/app-store-compliance ~/repositories/app-store-compliance bash ~/repositories/app-store-compliance/scripts/install.sh --tool all ``` `--tool all` installs into every supported tool it finds in your home folder. To pick one, pass its name instead. | Tool | Command | What it gets | One thing to do after | |---|---|---|---| | Claude Code | `install.sh` | Hook, skill, `/app-store-audit` | Restart Claude Code | | Codex CLI | `install.sh --tool codex` | Hook, skill | Run `/hooks` in Codex once and approve the new hook. Codex runs no new hook until you do | | Gemini CLI | `install.sh --tool gemini` | Hook, skill, `/app-store-audit` | Restart Gemini CLI. The hook works from 0.22, the skill needs 0.24 or later | | OpenCode | `install.sh --tool opencode` | Plugin, skill, `/app-store-audit` | Restart OpenCode | | Cursor | `install.sh --tool cursor` | Hook, skill | Restart Cursor | | GitHub Copilot CLI and Copilot in VS Code | `install.sh --tool copilot` | Hook, skill | Start a new Copilot CLI session and reload VS Code | | GitHub Copilot cloud agent and Copilot in JetBrains | `install.sh --tool copilot-repo --repo "/path/to/your/app"` | Hook in your app's `.github/hooks` | Commit `.github/hooks` to your default branch. The cloud agent reads hooks only from there | | Grok | `install.sh --tool grok` | Hook, skill | Start a new Grok session | | Qwen Code | `install.sh --tool qwen` | Hook, skill, in `$QWEN_HOME` when it is set | Restart Qwen Code | | Kimi Code | `install.sh --tool kimi` | Hook, skill | Restart Kimi Code | | Factory Droid | `install.sh --tool droid` | Hook, skill | Start a new Droid session | | Augment Auggie | `install.sh --tool auggie` | Hook, skill | Start a new Auggie session | | Windsurf | `install.sh --tool windsurf` | Hook, skill | Restart Windsurf | Every run ends with `Install verified.` only after it has fed a submit command to the hook in that tool's own payload format and seen it blocked. For OpenCode that check runs the plugin under node, so without node the run says `Installed, but not fully verified.` instead. If you see a `FAIL` line instead, fix that line and run the same command with `doctor` added. What it writes, so you can check it. - The guard, into that tool's own folder, for example `~/.codex/hooks/` or `~/.gemini/hooks/`. - The skill. Claude Code reads it from `~/.claude/skills/`. Every other tool reads one shared copy in `~/.agents/skills/`. - One hook entry in that tool's config (`~/.claude/settings.json`, `~/.codex/hooks.json`, `~/.gemini/settings.json`, `~/.cursor/hooks.json`, `~/.copilot/hooks/` or `$COPILOT_HOME/hooks/`), or for OpenCode one plugin file in `~/.config/opencode/plugins/`. Every other setting is kept, and a dated backup sits next to a file that already existed. A config that is not valid JSON or repeats a key is never rewritten. You get the exact block to paste instead. - For Gemini CLI it also turns on `tools.enableHooks`, which Gemini needs before version 0.26 to run any hook. - For Kimi Code it appends one marked `[[hooks]]` block to `~/.kimi-code/config.toml` (or `$KIMI_CODE_HOME/config.toml`) and never rewrites or prints the rest of that file, which can hold API keys. Uninstall removes exactly that block. - For Factory Droid it writes to `~/.factory/settings.json` when your hooks already live there, because Droid ignores them once `~/.factory/hooks.json` exists. #### Tools the installer does not wire, and what to do instead Each of these was checked against its own documentation. Where a tool can block a command but its format could not be confirmed, you get the manual step rather than a guess. | Tool | What to do | |---|---| | Kiro CLI | Kiro sends the event as JSON on stdin and blocks the tool when a `PreToolUse` command hook exits non-zero, and the guard reads Kiro's `shell`, `execute_bash`, `execute_pwsh` and `execute_cmd` payloads. The installer does not wire it yet. After `install.sh`, add `.kiro/hooks/app-store-compliance.json` to the project with `{"version":"v1","hooks":[{"name":"app-store-compliance","trigger":"PreToolUse","matcher":"^(shell\|execute_bash\|execute_pwsh\|execute_cmd)$","action":{"type":"command","command":"bash ~/.claude/hooks/app-store-compliance-guard.sh"}}]}`. Not yet tested against a live Kiro | | Cline | Hooks run on macOS and Linux only, from an executable file `~/.cline/hooks/PreToolUse` that answers `{"cancel":true}`. Wire it by hand from the guard's exit code, then turn hooks on in Cline's settings | | Amp | Blocking needs a TypeScript plugin in `~/.config/amp/plugins/`. Not installed automatically yet. Run the guard by hand before a submit | | Goose, Crush | Both can block, and their file layout could not be confirmed. Run the guard by hand before a submit | | Roo Code, Continue | No hook, only a deny list. Add the submit commands (`fastlane`, `xcrun altool`, `eas submit`, `gradle bundleRelease`) to Roo's `deniedCommands` or to the exclude list in Continue's `permissions.yaml` | | Aider, Copilot for Xcode | No way to run a check before a command. Run the guard by hand, or as a git pre-push hook, before every submit | It never touches your GitHub account or your credentials. Undo it with the same command and `uninstall`, for example `install.sh --tool gemini uninstall`. The shared skill stays until the last tool using

details.readme:
The open-source Claude Motion & CapCut alternative

Install · Agents · Use cases & remakes · Why OpenMotion · Setup & architecture · Community

**English** · [简体中文](docs/README.zh-CN.md) · [日本語](docs/README.ja.md)
# OpenMotion OpenMotion is a **full-stack agentic video** studio and an **open-source alternative to Claude Motion and CapCut**. Upload a reference video or paste a social video link to **recreate it with your own brand kit and copy**. - 🎬 **Full-stack video recreation.** Code video with HTML. Your agent breaks down the reference, rebuilds its shots and transitions, and generates missing assets. Edit the timing in Studio and render an MP4 from the same project. - 🔑 **BYOA — Bring Your Own Agent. BYOK — Bring Your Own Keys.** OpenMotion is free and open source. Recreate videos in [your local agent](#agent-wall) with your own API keys. Supported agents include Claude Code, Codex, and WorkBuddy. - 🧩 OpenMotion introduces **Motion.md**, a Markdown format for shot order, timing and transitions. Use it to share how a brand film works, shot by shot. - 🎛️ **Images, video, music and voice.** Create artwork with GPT Image 2.6, add a shot with Seedance 2.5, score it with Suno and narrate it with Eleven v4. [Explore the models and providers](#model-wall). ### Install from ChatGPT Marketplace **One-click installation. No manual configuration required.** Once installed, create motion videos from scratch, recreate reference videos, or start from a template—all in your conversation. **[Install OpenMotion in ChatGPT →](https://chatgpt.com/plugins/plugins_6a742d13e88481919b42002864b1bb26)** ### Install in your agent Install the main Skill with the [Skills CLI](https://github.com/vercel-labs/skills): ```sh npx skills add nexu-io/openmotion --skill openmotion ``` Then ask your agent: **Use OpenMotion to install and connect the local Studio and MCP, then help me make a video.** The Skill completes the source setup below when needed and reuses an existing workspace. Installing the Skill alone copies instructions; it does not yet install Studio or connect MCP. Copy this instruction into your local agent to set up OpenMotion from source: ```text Read https://github.com/nexu-io/openmotion/blob/main/docs/install.md and follow the instructions to install and connect OpenMotion in the current agent. ``` After setup, the agent opens the local template library and shows the welcome followed by three project-preview cards in a self-contained HTML document. Each installation samples three distinct entries from the curated pool of four. The complete silent previews and posters are bundled, so this display does not wait for native MCP reload or fetch remote reference films. Native original-reference playback remains available separately and requires internet access. The library opens once using the opening tool's result, with no extra page or playback audit. An opening failure is reported with a usable link and does not invalidate installation. Automatic current-chat MCP activation is assessed independently. Preview a card, choose **Recreate template**, then send your brief to start creating. [Source installation guide](docs/install.md) · [Onboarding selection](docs/install.md#maintained-recommendation-selection) ### Install the published npm app (optional) Source setup above remains the default for repository installation. To explicitly choose the published application with prebuilt Studio and its configured online catalog, copy this instruction into your local agent: ```text Read https://releases.open-design.ai/motion and follow the instructions to install and connect the published npm application in the current agent. ``` [Published application installation and channel selection](docs/install.md). details.readme:
# Estella **A 2D and 3D game engine whose editor is an MCP server.**
Your AI agent builds the game with the same 181 tools the editor's own UI uses — then ships it to the web, mini-game platforms, playable ads, desktop and native mobile. [![License: Apache 2.0](https://img.shields.io/badge/License-Apache_2.0-blue.svg)](LICENSE) [![Release](https://img.shields.io/github/v/release/esengine/estella)](https://github.com/esengine/estella/releases) [![MCP](https://img.shields.io/badge/MCP-181_tools-8A2BE2.svg)](https://estellaengine.com/docs/agents/mcp/) [![Platform](https://img.shields.io/badge/Platform-Web%20%7C%20Mini--games%20%7C%20Playable%20ads%20%7C%20Desktop%20%7C%20Android%20%7C%20iOS-green.svg)](https://estellaengine.com/docs/publishing/overview/) [![Ask DeepWiki](https://img.shields.io/badge/Ask-DeepWiki-1f6feb.svg)](https://deepwiki.com/esengine/estella) [Website](https://estellaengine.com)  ·  [Agent](#your-agent-drives-the-editor)  ·  [Getting Started](#getting-started)  ·  [Documentation](#documentation)  ·  [QQ群 481923584](https://qm.qq.com/q/BONa5LXQ0U)
Every frame is one MCP tool call into the editor, captured as it happened — no mouse involved.
## Your agent drives the editor The Estella editor speaks the **Model Context Protocol**. Connect Claude Code, Cursor, Codex or any MCP client, and the agent works inside the real editor rather than around it: - **It builds** — creates projects, spawns entities from the editor's own Create catalog, writes component fields, makes prefabs, paints tilemaps, writes and type-checks scripts. - **It looks** — takes screenshots of the viewport and the running game, replays a frame draw by draw, compares the game with reference images, and audits what a scene's look lacks. - **It plays** — enters Play mode, steps time deterministically, sends input and clicks UI by name, runs scripted playtests, then reads the running world back. - **It makes assets** — images, sound effects, music and 3D models, each answered with a picture of what it made. - **It ships** — reads project health, exports the game, and drives a build running on a connected phone. Every call goes through the editor's command surface: each one is **one undo step**, you watch it happen in the window, and you can take the mouse back at any time. The editor starts **read-only**; an agent edits only after you allow it in *Window → Connect AI Tools…*, which also writes the client's MCP config for you. **The tools are not all loaded at once.** A session starts with the everyday ones only, about fifty: read and edit the scene, play and step the game, open and save, screenshots, logs, undo. The rest sit in the groups below, and the agent lists a group when the work calls for it (`enable_tools { groups: ["look"] }`), so a session does not pay thousands of tokens of tool descriptions for tools it never uses. Long tool guides work the same way: a description is the short form, and `tool_guide` reads the rest by topic. How a kind of task is done end to end (2D and 3D gameplay, UI, animation, multiplayer, performance, shipping) is a skill the agent reads with `skill_guide` before it starts. | Group | What the agent gets | |---|---| | core | scene tree, entities, components, play / step / input, screenshots, logs, undo | | `assets` · `prefab` · `authoring` | asset documents and import settings, tilemaps, prefabs and variants, physics bodies, UI events | | `look` · `render` | reference images beside the game, light and field sweeps, frame capture and replay, shadows, LOD, bakes | | `code` · `project` | scripts, symbol search, type-check, project settings, health, export | | `image` · `sound` · `modeling` | draw sprites and textures, compose sound and music, build 3D models from steps | | `terrain` · `tripo` | shape land from steps (ranges, rivers, roads, a coast) and place it in the scene; generate textured 3D models with Tripo AI (your own key and credits) | | `play` · `view` · `device` | gamepads, time scale, scripted playtests, editor view, and a game running on a connected phone | **How undo works.** Tools are sorted by how their effect is taken back, not by what they touch: | A call that… | is taken back by | |---|---| | reads (scene tree, screenshots, logs, stats) | nothing to take back | | plays, steps or sends input to the game | **Stop**: the game runs in its own copy of the world and never touches the scene you edit | | edits the scene or a prefab | **Undo**: the edit goes through the editor's own history, the one Ctrl+Z walks | | writes project files (a script, an asset, an image, a material) | **Undo** as well: the editor keeps each file as it was before the call and puts it back | | leaves the project or runs code nobody can enumerate (a new project, an export, an editor command, code evaluated in the running game) | not undoable, and marked so | One call is one step however much it did: a tool that adds six entities and writes two files is undone by a single Undo, by you with Ctrl+Z or by the agent with its `undo` tool. A save is not a step, so undoing never rolls a saved file back under an unchanged scene. → [Connecting an agent](https://estellaengine.com/docs/agents/mcp/) ## Why Estella, when Unity and Unreal have MCP too? An MCP server can be bolted onto any editor. What an agent can actually get done depends on what sits behind it. - **The protocol is the editor, not a plugin on it.** The 181 tools call the pipelines the editor's own menus, inspector and toolbar run, so an agent's edit is the edit a person would have made, and undoes the same way. Calls are schema-checked and permission-gated by the editor itself. - **The agent can check its own work.** It steps a paused game frame by frame, so "play three seconds, then look" is the same frame every run. It sees the game, not just the log: screenshots, a frame replayed draw call by draw call, the game set beside a reference image, scripted playtests that read the running world back. - **The agent can make what the game needs.** Sprites, textures, sound effects, music and 3D models come from tools inside the editor, so a prototype does not stop at grey boxes while someone opens five other programs. - **Everything is text.** Scenes, prefabs and materials are JSON; gameplay is TypeScript. An agent reads and writes the project directly, and every change is a reviewable diff. - **It ships where heavier engines struggle.** A WebAssembly runtime that loads on a phone browser, seven Chinese mini-game platforms, single-file playable ads for the major ad networks, and native Android / iOS apps — from one project. - **It is open.** The runtime, SDK, pipeline and CLI are Apache-2.0: no royalties, no seats, no runtime fees. The editor is a free download. ## Rendered in real time

One day on the Amazon Lumberyard Bistro, recorded frame by frame from the running game: a sun that follows the clock, weather that turns from clear to mist, rain and snow, baked bounce light, reflections and volumetric haze. Scene © Amazon Lumberyard, CC BY 4.0, modified.

Space Frigate, a game made with Estella and recorded frame by frame as it runs: flying on thrusters, gunnery, and a jump through a gate to another star system. Every model, texture and sound in it is generated from a recipe.

A fight scene an AI agent built in the editor through MCP, recorded frame by frame as it runs. Both characters, their rigs and animations, the columns, the braziers and the floor texture were generated with Tripo AI by the editor's tripo tools.
## What's inside Estella is a C++ engine with a TypeScript SDK. The core runs as WebAssembly on the web and natively on desktop and mobile; game logic is written as ECS systems in TypeScript. **2D** — sprites and sprite animation, tilemaps (with LDtk import), Spine 2.1 – 4.3 and DragonBones, 2D lights and shadows, UI with layout, rich and bitmap text, particles, Box2D physics, native 2D rigs. **3D** — glTF / FBX import, PBR materials, directional / point / spot lights with shadows, sky atmosphere with time of day and weather, baked lightmaps, light and reflection probes, SSR, SSGI, height fog, terrain, water, foliage, skeletal animation with spri

details.readme:
A lightweight 2.5D character player for the web, with lip sync and webcam face tracking. A few lines of code put a character in a page, a stream overlay or an app.
Comes with 25 featured characters in different styles, ready to use.

English · 中文 · 日本語 · Tiếng Việt

- WebGL2, no dependencies, about 30 KB gzipped for the core - Lip sync (microphone, audio, video) and webcam face tracking (MediaPipe), both in the browser, imported only when you need them - Plays LivLiv, VRM and PNGTuber characters through the same API - Full-body characters stand on the ground: they sway, crouch and dip with their feet in place, in the shot you pick - 25 featured characters in [`characters/`](characters/), ready to use ## Try it - **Online**: the examples run on [livliv-dev.github.io/player](https://livliv-dev.github.io/player/). - **Here**: `npm install && npm run build`, serve this folder with any static server and open `/example/demo.html` (expressions, actions, microphone, camera; `?model=../characters//` picks another character). `/example/png.html` and `/example/vrm.html` show a PNGTuber and a VRM. - **On livliv.ai**: each character's page there plays it with the same renderer. Start at [livliv.ai/discover](https://livliv.ai/discover). ## Project LivLiv We want the art of creating characters to belong to everyone. We're open-sourcing our AI tools for character creation, [the player and its playback protocol](https://github.com/livliv-dev/player), and [a stage where your characters can meet an audience](https://github.com/livliv-dev/stage). Come say hello on [Discord](https://discord.gg/ac5qF36T2H) and follow us on [X (Twitter)](https://x.com/livliv_ai). ## Use it in your page ```sh npm install @livliv-dev/player ``` ```js import { Player } from '@livliv-dev/player' const player = new Player(document.querySelector('canvas')) await player.load('characters/k01/') // a folder with model.json and textures/, or a .livliv file player.setExpression('smile') // ids are in player.expressions player.act('nod') player.params.mouthOpen = 0.6 // 0..1 ``` Lip sync and face tracking: ```js import { createSpeech } from '@livliv-dev/player/voice' import { startFaceTracking } from '@livliv-dev/player/tracking' // needs @mediapipe/tasks-vision const speech = createSpeech(player) button.onclick = () => { speech.unlock(); speech.say('/reply.mp3') } await startFaceTracking(player) ``` A VRM or a PNGTuber, on the same API: ```js import { BodyPlayer } from '@livliv-dev/player/body' import { VrmBody } from '@livliv-dev/player/vrm' // needs three and @pixiv/three-vrm import { PngBody } from '@livliv-dev/player/png' const vrm = new BodyPlayer(canvasA, new VrmBody()) await vrm.load('/avatars/me.vrm') const png = new BodyPlayer(canvasB, new PngBody()) await png.load({ closed: 'me-closed.png', open: 'me-open.png' }) ``` The whole API is in [API.md](API.md): options, params, expressions and actions, drivers, recorded poses and attachment points, VRM and PNGTuber characters, the limits on untrusted files, the model package and the format version. The LivLiv package format (`.livliv`, `model.json` v4) is in [FORMAT.md](FORMAT.md), with a JSON Schema in [`schema/`](schema/); packages exported before v4 are described in [FORMAT-v3.md](FORMAT-v3.md) and still play. > The npm package is the player alone. The featured characters are in this repository's [`characters/`](characters/): copy > the ones you use next to your page, with their licence. ## Featured characters `characters/` holds 25 characters, ready to `load()`. Most were made by LivLiv: use them free with credit ("Characters: LivLiv (livliv.ai)"), commercially too if you are an individual. Don't sell them or merchandise made from them, and don't train AI models on them. They are **not** covered by the Apache License; the terms are in [characters/LICENSE.md](characters/LICENSE.md). Kujira, Kujira Q and Pen come from other people's work, with their own terms in [characters/CREDITS.md](characters/CREDITS.md). **New in 0.5.0: full-body characters.** Drawn head to feet, they stand on the ground: they sway, crouch and dip while their feet stay put. Four featured characters are full-body: Tsubaki, Neve, Juno and Viola (f05–f08). Pick the shot with `player.view.fit`: `'frame'` (default), `'knee'` or `'whole'`; see [Full-body characters](API.md#full-body-characters) in API.md. Each character has a `cover.webp`, its first frame: `player.load(source, { poster })` shows it until the character is ready, and [example/loading.js](example/loading.js) shows it before any script has run. Each character is also one file to download, `.livliv`, at `https://livliv-dev.github.io/player/characters/.livliv` (the names below link to them). They are served with CORS, so a page on another site can `load()` one straight from there, and [`index.json`](https://livliv-dev.github.io/player/characters/index.json) lists them all. | id | name | id | name | id | name | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | `k01` | [Sena](https://livliv-dev.github.io/player/characters/k01.livliv) | `d01` | [Yui](https://livliv-dev.github.io/player/characters/d01.livliv) | `v01` | [Aster](https://livliv-dev.github.io/player/characters/v01.livliv) | | `k02` | [Elio](https://livliv-dev.github.io/player/characters/k02.livliv) | `d02` | [Leo](https://livliv-dev.github.io/player/characters/d02.livliv) | `v03` | [Mira](https://livliv-dev.github.io/player/characters/v03.livliv) | | `char06` | [Aoi](https://livliv-dev.github.io/player/characters/char06.livliv) | `d03` | [Nana](https://livliv-dev.github.io/player/characters/d03.livliv) | `v04` | [Kai](https://livliv-dev.github.io/player/characters/v04.livliv) | | `char07` | [Sora](https://livliv-dev.github.io/player/characters/char07.livliv) | `d03ft` | [Nana (refined)](https://livliv-dev.github.io/player/characters/d03ft.livliv) | `v05` | [Lilith](https://livliv-dev.github.io/player/characters/v05.livliv) | | `s01` | [Hana](https://livliv-dev.github.io/player/characters/s01.livliv) | `p01` | [Kujira](https://livliv-dev.github.io/player/characters/p01.livliv) | `v06` | [Usa](https://livliv-dev.github.io/player/characters/v06.livliv) | | `q02` | [Mochi](https://livliv-dev.github.io/player/characters/q02.livliv) | `p02` | [Kujira Q](https://livliv-dev.github.io/player/characters/p02.livliv) | `v07` | [Stella](https://livliv-dev.github.io/player/characters/v07.livliv) | | `q03` | [Kotaro](https://livliv-dev.github.io/player/characters/q03.livliv) | `p03` | [Pen](https://livliv-dev.github.io/player/characters/p03.livliv) | `w01` | [Max](https://livliv-dev.github.io/player/characters/w01.livliv) | | `f05` | [Tsubaki (full-body)](https://livliv-dev.github.io/player/characters/f05.livliv) | `f06` | [Neve (full-body)](https://livliv-dev.github.io/player/characters/f06.livliv) | `f07` | [Juno (full-body)](https://livliv-dev.github.io/player/characters/f07.livliv) | | `f08` | [Viola (full-body)](https://livliv-dev.github.io/player/characters/f08.livliv) | | | | | ## Characters of your own You can bring in a PNGTuber's pictures, or a VRM (drawn with three.js); or make a character of your own from one picture on [livliv.ai](https://livliv.ai). - **A PNGTuber**: two pictures (mouth closed, mouth open), and two more with the eyes closed if you have them. - **A VRM**: from VRoid Studio or any tool that exports VRM 0.x or 1.0. - **A LivLiv model**: make one from a picture on [livliv.ai](https://livliv.ai), then download its model package from the character's page (**Model package**): a `.livliv` file. Pass it to `load()` as it is (a URL, or the `File` someone picked), or unzipped as a folder. Full-body characters play too (from 0.5); livliv.ai does not offer their packages yet. ## About the player and the characters LivLiv Player and the `.livliv` format are LivLiv's own work. They use no Live2D software or Cubism SDK and do not read `.moc3` or `.cmo3` files. "Live2D" is a trademark of Live2D Inc.; LivLiv is not affiliated with it. Making a character on livliv.ai uses AI. The player itself only plays: it calls no AI service and reads only the files you point it at. Face tracking runs Google's MediaPipe in the browser, and camera images stay on the device; API.md has the networking details. The featured characters in this repository were made on LivLiv too, also with AI; Kujira, Kujira Q and Pen adapt other people's characters ([credits](characters/CREDITS.md)). Refined Nana (`d03ft`) also has swinging parts and head-turn keyforms added with LivLiv's own tools. A package's `meta.author` and `meta.license` record who made it and on what terms: keep them and follow them. When you show a character made with LivLiv in public, say that AI was used to make it, and don't present it as hand-drawn or hand-rigged. ## Embed without code ```html ``` The same `/live/` page has a transparent background and works as an OBS Browser Source.\ (Powered by [https://livliv.ai](https://livliv.ai)) ## Develop ```sh git clone https://github.com/livliv-dev/player cd player npm install npm run check # types npm run build # dist/: index.js, tracking.js, voice.js, body.js, png.js, vrm.js (ES modules), chunks/ and types/ npm test # unit and fuzz tests (Node 22.18 or newer, no browser) npm run test:browser # every featured character drawn in headless Chromium; once: npx playwright-core install chromium-headless-shell npm run test:engines # a sample on Firefox and WebKit, where WebGL2 starts (a GPU or a software GL); once: npx playwright-core install firefox webkit ``` `src/runtime/` is the renderer and motion code livliv.ai runs; this repository is published from it. See [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md). Security reports: [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md). ## Browser support WebGL2 and ES2023: Chrome / Edge 97+, Firefox 104+, Safari 15.4+. Tested on current desktop browsers, not yet on phones. ## License The code is under the [Apache License 2.0](LICENSE) (see also [NOTICE](NOTICE)). The featured characters have their own licence, [characters/LICENSE.md](characters/LICENSE.md). You may keep the LivLiv name and logo in your own versions, as long as they don't claim to be the official one. ## Thanks Thanks to 上善无形, ZipZipPipe and 贱兔死顺盖, whose characters Kujira, Kujira Q and Pen are based on: see [characters/CREDITS.md](characters/CREDITS.md).

details.readme:
# Jev-Interaction **System-One-controlled full-duplex voice interaction.**
Turn-taking as decisions you write — not a model you train. [中文](README.zh-CN.md) · [Cookbook](cookbook) · [Profiles](jev_interaction/profiles) · [Decisions](jev_interaction/judge/questions.py) · [Docs](#documentation) 🏆 **Build of the Week** at [TypeSafe](https://typesafe.ai) · 🤗 **Live demo** on [Hugging Face](https://huggingface.co/spaces/pupunpu/Jev-Interaction) [![Build of the Week](https://img.shields.io/badge/%F0%9F%8F%86%20Build%20of%20the%20Week-TypeSafe-f5b301)](https://typesafe.ai) [![Hugging Face Space](https://img.shields.io/badge/%F0%9F%A4%97%20Hugging%20Face-live%20demo-ffcc4d)](https://huggingface.co/spaces/pupunpu/Jev-Interaction) [![PyPI](https://img.shields.io/pypi/v/jev-interaction)](https://pypi.org/project/jev-interaction/) [![tests](https://github.com/native-bond-lab/Jev-Interaction/actions/workflows/tests.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/native-bond-lab/Jev-Interaction/actions/workflows/tests.yml) ![python](https://img.shields.io/badge/python-3.10%2B-3776ab) ![license](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-Apache--2.0-blue) ![status](https://img.shields.io/badge/status-alpha-f59e0b) ![judge](https://img.shields.io/badge/judge-Jev-0f766e) ![duplex](https://img.shields.io/badge/full--duplex-voice-6366f1)
*Most of a conversation happens in the gaps: who waits, who yields, who answers with nothing but an "mm-hm".
We wrote every gap down as a question, and gave the questions to Jev.* Try it here: [Try it now](https://pupunpu-jev-interaction.hf.space/) (or [on Hugging Face](https://huggingface.co/spaces/pupunpu/Jev-Interaction)).
> **Built on [Jev](https://typesafe.ai).** Every turn-taking decision here is a question Jev answers in tens of > milliseconds. Without it, none of this would work. > **From an applied lab.** Native Bond Lab is the applied research lab behind a consumer voice product. Everything in > this repository comes out of that product and runs at scale on real calls with real users, not in a demo. ![Jev-Interaction architecture](docs/architecture.svg) **Full duplex from a cascade.** Speech recognition → Jev's decisions → any language model → any speech synthesis. The agent listens while it talks, says "mm-hm" while you talk, lets a pause stand, carries on through a backchannel, yields or finishes its sentence when you cut in, and picks the call back up after a silence. **A System One for conversation.** People on a call run two minds at once: a fast one that knows, without thinking, when to wait, when to yield and when to say "mm-hm", and a slow one that works out what to say. Here Jev is the fast mind, deciding each moment in tens of milliseconds; the language model is the slow one, writing the words. Neither waits for the other. Voice agents today take one of two roads. **Cascades** bolt a small trained model onto that pipeline to guess *"has the user finished?"* and leave everything else to timers. **End-to-end full-duplex models** (Moshi, GPT-4o Realtime, Gemini Live) learn turn-taking inside one large speech model: fast and natural, but a black box. You cannot see why it stopped, cannot change how it takes turns for a product or a persona, and are tied to the vendor's model, voices and session limits. **Jev-Interaction keeps the cascade's freedom and gives it the judgement.** Every one of those moments becomes an explicit decision: a plain-language multiple-choice question, a probability from Jev for every choice, and a policy that turns the probabilities into an action. Questions, policies and the agent's manner are text you can read, change and replay against real calls. **Demo video: on the way.** ## Quickstart From PyPI, in any folder; the page walks you through each provider and key: ```bash pip install "jev-interaction[server]" # add ,sound for the sound model and ,voiceprint for the caller's voiceprint jev-interaction serve # http://localhost:8080 ``` Or from a clone, one command installs everything, starts the server and opens the page: ```bash git clone https://github.com/native-bond-lab/Jev-Interaction && cd Jev-Interaction ./scripts/setup.sh # --china installs through a domestic PyPI mirror ``` Or with Docker (any OS): ```bash cp .env.example .env # fill it in, or leave it empty and use the setup steps on the page docker compose up # http://localhost:8080 ``` Open . Setup goes one node at a time: the judge (Jev), a language model, speech recognition, a voice. Paste a key and the page recognises whose it is; pick the language model from the endpoint's own model list; test each step before moving on. Settings are saved to `.env` in the folder you started from. Make a persona of your own or change one with **New persona** / **Edit** under the cards (on your own machine or your own Docker; a public deployment does not offer it): who it is for the language model, its habits on a call for Jev, its turn-taking and its voice, saved to `profiles/`. Then pick a persona and click the orb to call (click it again to hang up). The voice detector is TEN VAD, the one our product runs on; headphones still give the cleanest call. Each node and its providers, the recommended setups (global and mainland China), presets and publishing a Hugging Face Space: [docs/setup.md](docs/setup.md). ### In your own code ```python from jev_interaction import Config, Profile from jev_interaction.adapters import best_vad from jev_interaction.adapters.openai_compat import OpenAICompatResponder from jev_interaction.adapters.scribe import ScribeRealtime from jev_interaction.judge import JevClient from jev_interaction.session import Session session = Session( Profile.load("support") # a built-in persona, or a path to your own YAML, send=my_send, # async: deliver events to your client judge=JevClient(), recognizer=ScribeRealtime(language="en"), responder=OpenAICompatResponder(), # any OpenAI-compatible endpoint vad=best_vad(), # TEN VAD (pip install ten-vad), or the energy detector without it config=Config(language="en"), ) await session.start() await session.on_audio(frame) # 200 ms of 16 kHz PCM16, as it arrives await session.on_client({"type": "playback", "state": "idle"}) ``` Events to the client: `line`, `listen`, `stop`, `finish_line`, `persona`, `hangup`, plus `user`, `pace` and `decision` for display. Client messages: `playback` and `heard`. ### Inside a coding agent In Claude Code or DeepSeek Harness, a slash command brings up a voice companion for the session you are in: you talk to the computer, it hands what you ask for to the session as a background task, says how far it has got when you ask, tells you when it is done, and sleeps in between. The talking is done by a fast model of the harness's own that you choose the first time, speech recognition and synthesis by providers of your choice; there is no page and no window. ```bash pipx install "jev-interaction[server,local]" # Claude Code: /plugin marketplace add native-bond-lab/Jev-Interaction # /plugin install interaction@jev-interaction then /interaction:start # DeepSeek Harness: dsh plugin --profile tui add /connectors/deepseek-harness then /interaction ``` Setup, how it works and what is still open: [docs/harness.md](docs/harness.md). Background tasks and sleep in your own code (`Session(executors=...)`): [docs/tasks.md](docs/tasks.md). ## How it works ![The call policy: the ears give signals, everything goes on one timeline, who is making sound picks one of four moments, Jev answers small facts, thresholds pick one action, the language model writes the words](docs/policy.svg) Jev-Interaction is an interaction engine, not a voice-activity detector. Jev never hears audio and never decides that someone is speaking; the ears do that (voice activity, the recognizer, a sound model, a voiceprint) and their output is only signals. What the engine decides is what to do with the moment: answer, wait, slip in an "mm-hm", cut in, carry on over an interruption, pick a quiet up, hang up. Three principles shape it. 1. **Two parties, four moments.** The agent and the user each make sound or not, which gives four moments: the user has the turn, both are quiet, both are talking, the agent is talking. Each moment has its own set of actions, and nothing else. 2. **One timeline, one "now".** The call is one record that only grows: the words, the signals, every answer from Jev, every action taken, each on the same clock (`Ledger`). Every judgement and the model that writes the lines read the same present from it (`judge/state.py`, `Now`); no decision keeps its own account of the call. 3. **One action per moment, no case left out.** In any moment there is one set of choices that do not overlap, and every situation belongs to exactly one of them. One answer from Jev, one thing done. | moment | Jev is asked | one action | |---|---|---| | the user has the turn | have they finished · which pace (one yes/no fact per pace) · is something they asked for due · sparring or telling | take the turn (when the words and the sound agree) · cut in (in a pace that does) · slip in a sound · stay silent | | quiet | does the agent's last line leave them a move · did they say they need a moment · were goodbyes said · has the agent called out with no answer | let it be · pick the thread up · check on them · hang up (the facts and the clock decide) | | both talking | what their words over the line are: a reaction, a "stop", or something of their own | carry on · stop and listen · finish the sentence · take the floor back · react at once | | the agent is talking | nothing | nothing to decide | What follows from the principles, the paces, and the same engine under two personas: [docs/policy.md](docs/policy.md). ## What you get - **Every piece is yours to choose.** The intelligence (any language model), the voice (any synthesizer and voice), the style, the task and the persona. The persona reaches the interaction itself, not only the words: an impatient character cuts in and answers half-sentences, a gentle one says "mm-hm" often and waits you out, a tutor finishes the explanation before yielding, a support agent stays brief and stops the moment you speak. - **The pace routes itself, turn by turn.** Each turn Jev also judges which pace the call is in: normal conversation, listening (the caller is pouring something out: more listening sounds, longer waits, fewer interruptions), narrating (the agent is telling a story: an "mm-hm" does not stop it) or eager (quick to take the floor). One call moves between them on its own, from small talk into a game and back. - **A new task is a few knobs, zero-shot.** Nothing here is trained on any benchmark or on your data. A task profile is a page of text; the pause problem in Full-Duplex-Bench was fixed with two knobs, and each trade-off is measured, not guessed. - **Every number comes with a reason.** Each decision is logged with the state Jev read and the probabilities it gave, so a bad moment points at the step that caused it, and a reworded question can be replayed against recorded calls before it ships. - **Calls of any length.** No session is held open on a model provider; each decision and each reply is a fresh request over a text history. - **Cheap.** A decision is a few hundred tokens to Jev; in our runs a reply cost about $0.002 of language model and a 400-sample benchmark round about $2. ## Task profiles One framework, many products. A profile says what the agent is for, how it behaves on a call, and how each decision is read. | profile | listening sounds | mid-sentence pauses
